title: Occupied France, 1942–1944
setting: France, spring 1942, nearly two years after the defeat. The Germans occupy the north and the whole Atlantic coast; the south is the free zone, governed from the spa town of Vichy by Marshal Pétain's French State, which works with the occupier. A guarded demarcation line divides them. Food, coal and clothes are rationed, curfews empty the streets, and posters name the hostages shot after each attack. A scattered, divided Resistance prints newspapers, hides people and gathers intelligence, and London speaks to it every evening on the BBC.

regions.name: France
regions.label: country
regions.status: divided by the armistice of June 1940
regions.lore: A defeated country cut into zones: the occupied north and west, the free zone in the south under Vichy, Alsace and Moselle annexed in all but name, and the Nord and Pas-de-Calais run from Brussels. Nearly two million French soldiers are still prisoners in Germany.

regions.name: Greater German Reich
regions.label: country
regions.lore: Germany, with Austria, Luxembourg and the conquered lands of the east. Nearly a million French prisoners of war work there.

regions.name: Britain
regions.label: country
regions.status: at war; the BBC speaks to France every evening
regions.lore: Still fighting. General de Gaulle's Free France is in London, and the BBC's French broadcasts and their coded personal messages are listened to in secret all over France.

regions.name: The Channel Islands
regions.label: country
regions.lore: The British islands off the coast of Normandy, occupied by the Germans since 1940 and fortified.

regions.name: Spain
regions.label: country
regions.status: neutral; escapers end up in the camp at Miranda
regions.lore: Franco's Spain, neutral but friendly to Germany. Escapers who cross the Pyrenees are often jailed, then let go towards Gibraltar and Britain.

regions.name: Switzerland
regions.label: country
regions.status: neutral; the border is watched
regions.lore: Neutral, surrounded, and full of spies and refugees. Its border guards turn many refugees back.

regions.name: Italy
regions.label: country
regions.lore: Mussolini's Italy, Germany's ally. It claims Nice, Savoy and Corsica.

regions.name: French Algeria
regions.label: country
regions.status: loyal to Vichy
regions.lore: French Algeria, governed loyally for Vichy. Ships from Marseille still cross to Algiers.

regions.name: Occupied Zone
regions.label: zone
regions.status: under the German military command in Paris
regions.lore: The north, Paris and the whole Atlantic coast, under the German military command at the Hôtel Majestic. Clocks run on German time, the curfew empties the streets, and the coast is a forbidden zone of bunkers.

regions.name: Free Zone
regions.label: zone
regions.status: governed from Vichy; no German troops
regions.lore: The south, governed from Vichy by the French State. No German soldiers in the streets, but the French police arrest communists, Gaullists and foreign Jews, and the camps at Gurs, Rivesaltes and Le Vernet are full. Lyon and Marseille are crowded with refugees.

regions.name: Nord and Pas-de-Calais (under Brussels)
regions.label: zone
regions.status: run by the German command in Brussels
regions.lore: The mining north, cut off from the rest of France and governed with Belgium by the German command in Brussels. Its miners struck in May 1941.

regions.name: Alsace and Moselle (annexed)
regions.label: zone
regions.status: annexed in all but name
regions.lore: Alsace and Moselle, taken back into the Reich in all but name: French is banned, names are germanised, thousands of "undesirables" have been expelled to France, and the border is closed to the French.

regions.name: Bouches-du-Rhône
regions.label: département
regions.lore: Marseille, Aix, the camp at Les Milles for foreigners, and the Camargue's marshes.

regions.name: Corse
regions.label: département
regions.lore: An island département of mountains and maquis, governed from Vichy and claimed by Italy.

regions.name: Haute-Savoie
regions.label: département
regions.lore: Mountains and lakes on the Swiss border, crossed at night by smugglers and refugees.

regions.name: Seine
regions.label: département
regions.status: Paris and its suburbs, the heart of the occupation
regions.lore: Paris and its ring of suburbs: the red belt of factories at Saint-Denis and Billancourt, the camp at Drancy, the execution ground at Mont-Valérien, the prison at Fresnes.

regions.name: Vichy
regions.label: city
regions.status: the capital of the French State
regions.lore: A spa town turned capital: ministries in the hotels, the Marshal at the Hôtel du Parc, diplomats, informers and petitioners in the parks.

regions.name: Menton
regions.label: town
regions.status: held by Italy since June 1940
regions.lore: The border town Italy took in June 1940, with a handful of villages above it: Italian law, Italian lessons in the schools.

regions.name: Paris
regions.label: city
regions.status: occupied; German signposts on every corner
regions.lore: Occupied since June 1940. German soldiers sightsee, the cafés and cabarets are full of uniforms, and the metro is the only way around. The French police do much of the occupier's work. Curfew at midnight; the last metro is the race of every evening.

regions.name: Hôtel-de-Ville (4th)
regions.label: arrondissement
regions.status: the French police at home
regions.lore: Hôtel-de-Ville and the Île de la Cité: the town hall, Notre-Dame and the Préfecture de police, home of the Brigades spéciales that hunt communists and the Resistance.

regions.name: Luxembourg (6th)
regions.label: arrondissement
regions.lore: Luxembourg: the Senate, the Latin Quarter's publishers, the military prison of Cherche-Midi and the Hôtel Lutetia, taken over by German military intelligence.

regions.name: Élysée (8th)
regions.label: arrondissement
regions.status: requisitioned
regions.lore: Élysée: the Champs-Élysées with German parades, requisitioned hotels and ministries, and the security police's offices in rue des Saussaies.

regions.name: Popincourt (11th)
regions.label: arrondissement
regions.status: crowded and watched
regions.lore: Popincourt: workshops, printers, small factories and crowded flats between the Bastille and Père-Lachaise, many of them home to immigrant families. The police rounded up hundreds of Jewish men here in August 1941.

regions.name: Passy (16th)
regions.label: arrondissement
regions.status: the occupiers' quarter
regions.lore: Passy, the rich west: the German military command at the Hôtel Majestic, the security police on avenue Foch, and in rue Lauriston the French gangsters who work for them.

regions.name: Butte-Montmartre (18th)
regions.label: arrondissement
regions.lore: Butte-Montmartre: the hill, its cabarets full of German soldiers on leave, and below it the Barbès metro station, where a German naval cadet was shot in August 1941.

regions.name: Lyon
regions.label: city
regions.status: crowded, watched, and the heart of the southern Resistance
regions.lore: France's silk city and the crossroads of the free zone, crowded with refugees, journalists and exiles. The southern movements have their headquarters here, the traboules let a person cross a district without touching the street, and the Vichy police are everywhere.

map.credit: Arrondissements and communes: IGN Admin Express via geo.api.gouv.fr (Licence Ouverte 2.0, Etalab), adapted; rivers outside the city: Natural Earth

regions.name: Terreaux and the Slopes (1st)
regions.label: arrondissement
regions.status: quiet streets with many ways through
regions.lore: The Terreaux and the slopes of the Croix-Rousse: the town hall, old silk workers' buildings and the traboules, covered passages through courtyards and stairwells from one street to the next.

regions.name: Presqu'île (2nd)
regions.label: arrondissement
regions.lore: The Presqu'île between the Rhône and the Saône: Place Bellecour, the shops of rue de la République, Perrache station and the Hôtel Terminus beside it.

regions.name: Part-Dieu and Villette (3rd)
regions.label: arrondissement
regions.lore: Part-Dieu and Villette: barracks, the railway, and the military prison at Montluc.

regions.name: Croix-Rousse (4th)
regions.label: arrondissement
regions.lore: The Croix-Rousse plateau, the silk workers' hill: tall windows for the looms, a market, and a long tradition of revolt.

regions.name: Vieux Lyon and Fourvière (5th)
regions.label: arrondissement
regions.lore: Vieux Lyon under Fourvière: Renaissance streets, the cathedral of Saint-Jean, more traboules, and Vaise's factories upriver.

regions.name: Marseille
regions.label: city
regions.status: the last open port; visas and smugglers
regions.lore: The great port of the free zone, crowded with refugees waiting for visas and ships to Algiers, Lisbon or the Americas, with gangsters running the black market and the docks. The Vichy police watch the cafés of the Canebière.

regions.name: Canebière and Belsunce
regions.label: district
regions.lore: The Canebière and Belsunce: cafés, hotels full of refugees, consulates' queues and Saint-Charles station at the top of its great stair.

regions.name: Le Panier and La Joliette
regions.label: district
regions.lore: Le Panier, the old quarter above the Old Port: narrow streets, stairs and courtyards, poor and crowded, where anyone can disappear.

summary: France under the German occupation, from the spring of 1942 to the liberation. Join a small Resistance cell in Paris or Lyon, or make your own story anywhere in France.
toneNote: Tense, quiet and human: most days are queues, curfews and lies told well; violence is sudden and costs everyone. Persecution is shown with gravity, never as spectacle.
rules: History runs on: the war's great events happen on their dates whatever the player does; the story is what ordinary people do inside them.
Papers are checked at stations, crossings and in the street. A forged paper passes a glance, not a careful look.
Arrest is the constant danger, from the German and the French police alike; anyone arrested may talk.
Violence is rare, sudden and costly: an attack on a German brings reprisals on hostages.
The persecution of Jews, foreigners and others is real and growing worse: show it with gravity, never as spectacle.

limit.text: is faint with hunger and can barely keep going

world.demarcation line: guarded; needs an Ausweis or a smuggler
world.Spanish frontier: closed; crossed on foot with a guide

factions.name: The German occupation
factions.desc: The military command in France, the army, and the security police and SD (everyone says "the Gestapo") who hunt the Resistance.
factions.stance: in control of the occupied zone; shoots hostages after attacks

factions.name: The French State (Vichy)
factions.desc: Marshal Pétain's government at Vichy, its prefects, police and gendarmes, governing the free zone and administering the occupied one under German orders.
factions.stance: collaborating, and proud of its "National Revolution"

factions.name: Kingdom of Italy
factions.desc: Germany's ally; holds Menton and a strip of the Alpine frontier since 1940.
factions.stance: an ally of Germany with claims on Nice, Savoy and Corsica

factions.name: The Resistance
factions.desc: Scattered movements, networks and communist groups: underground papers, escape lines, intelligence, a few armed attacks. Divided, and hunted.

factions.name: Free France
factions.desc: General de Gaulle's movement in London and the French territories that joined it, with its own forces and agents.
factions.stance: speaks to France on the BBC and sends agents in by night

factions.name: The Allies
factions.desc: Britain and its empire, the United States since December 1941, and the Soviet Union in the east.
factions.stance: bombing factories and ports; no landing yet

roles.label: Printer
roles.desc: Sets type and runs a press; can make a newspaper, a poster or a pass look right.

roles.label: Courier
roles.desc: Carries messages, papers and money by bicycle and train, and knows which stations are watched.

roles.label: Railway worker
roles.desc: Works the yards and the trains; knows the timetables, the signals and the guards.

roles.label: Nurse
roles.desc: Works at a hospital where the wounded and the hunted sometimes come in under other names.

roles.label: Student
roles.desc: At the university or a lycée; angry, idealistic, and watched by the police since the November 1940 march.

roles.label: Town hall clerk
roles.desc: Stamps identity cards and ration cards all day; has access to blanks and seals.

timeline.text: From London on the BBC, General de Gaulle called on the French to fight on.
Pétain's government signed the armistice: the north and the coast occupied, the south left to a French government.
Parliament gave Marshal Pétain full powers at Vichy; the Republic became the "French State".
Vichy's first statute on the Jews barred them from public service, teaching and the press.
Pétain met Hitler at Montoire and announced "the way of collaboration".
Germany invaded the Soviet Union; the French communists joined the Resistance in force.
French police sealed off the 11th arrondissement and took thousands of Jewish men to a new camp at Drancy.
After a German officer was shot in Nantes, the Germans shot forty-eight hostages.
After Pearl Harbor, Germany declared war on the United States.
The first train of deported Jews left Drancy for the east.
Pierre Laval returned to power at Vichy as head of the government, with the Germans' blessing.

groups.stance: Laval in charge; closer to Germany than ever

timeline.text: A German order: from 7 June every Jew over six in the occupied zone must wear a yellow star.
The BBC told of the Free French holding Bir Hakeim in the Libyan desert for two weeks against Rommel.
On the radio Laval said he wished for Germany's victory, and announced the "Relève": skilled workers to Germany in exchange for prisoners.
Before dawn French police began arresting thousands of foreign Jewish families across Paris; families were held for days in the Vélodrome d'Hiver.
Answering the BBC, crowds marched for Bastille Day in Lyon and Marseille in defiance of Vichy.
Canadian and British troops landed at Dieppe and were thrown back with terrible losses.
Vichy's police rounded up foreign Jews across the free zone and handed them over to the Germans.
A Vichy law made men of 18 to 50 liable for any work the government judges useful, including in Germany.
American and British troops landed in Morocco and Algeria. After brief fighting the French forces there joined them.
German troops crossed the demarcation line and occupied the free zone; Italian troops took the land east of the Rhône and Corsica. Vichy's army was disbanded.

region_status.status: occupied by the Germans and Italians since 11 November 1942

groups.stance: a government with no zone of its own left

timeline.text: As German tanks reached the port, the French fleet at Toulon scuttled itself rather than be taken.
Admiral Darlan, who had gone over to the Allies in Algiers, was shot dead by a young royalist.
Police and German troops sealed off Marseille's Old Port quarter, arrested thousands and ordered everyone out of the north side of the port.
German engineers began dynamiting the evacuated streets north of Marseille's Old Port.
Vichy created the Milice, a French paramilitary police to fight "terrorists", Jews and communists.

groups.stance: arming the Milice against the Resistance

timeline.text: Compulsory labour service: young men born in 1920, 1921 and 1922 must go to work in Germany. Many vanish instead, into the hills.

groups.stance: growing fast: the young are taking to the maquis

timeline.text: The demarcation line was lifted: the checkpoints between north and south came down.
The German and Italian armies in Tunisia surrendered.
In Algiers, de Gaulle and General Giraud formed a French Committee of National Liberation.
German police raided a doctor's house in Caluire, outside Lyon, and arrested several Resistance leaders meeting there.
Italy signed an armistice with the Allies. The Germans disarmed the Italian army in France and took over its zone.

groups.stance: out of the war; its army in France disarmed

timeline.text: Corsica was freed by its own Resistance and French troops landed from Algiers: the first French département liberated.
Armed maquisards marched through Oyonnax in uniform to lay a wreath on the war memorial, then vanished into the hills.
Twenty-two men of an immigrant Resistance group were shot at Mont-Valérien; red posters call them "the army of crime".
German troops and the Milice crushed the maquis on the plateau of Glières.
Allied bombers hit the rail yards at La Chapelle in northern Paris; hundreds of people were killed around them.
Marshal Pétain visited Paris; crowds gathered to see him at the town hall.
The Allies landed in Normandy. The BBC broadcast its messages all night, and all over France the Resistance rose against the railways and telephone lines.
SS troops massacred 643 people at Oradour-sur-Glane, a village near Limoges, and burned it to the ground.
The ruins of Caen were taken by British and Canadian troops after six weeks of battle.
German gliders landed on the Vercors plateau, where thousands of maquisards had declared a free republic; the plateau fell within days.
American armour broke through at Avranches and poured into Brittany and the Loire country.
Most of Brittany and the Loire was freed by the Americans and the Breton maquis; the Germans held on in Brest, Lorient and Saint-Nazaire.
French and American troops landed in Provence between Toulon and Cannes.
The Paris police went on strike and occupied the Préfecture; the Resistance rose across the city and barricades went up.

groups.stance: fighting in the streets of Paris

timeline.text: As the Germans pulled out of the southwest, the Resistance took Toulouse, Limoges and the towns between.
The Germans took Marshal Pétain from Vichy by force and drove him east, towards Germany.
Paris was liberated: General Leclerc's French armoured division entered the city and the German commander surrendered.
Marseille and Toulon were freed by French troops after a week of fighting; the Germans in the Alps and along the Rhône fell back north.
The Germans left Bordeaux; the Resistance took over the city and the southwest coast, except for the fortresses of Royan and La Rochelle.
Allied armies raced through the north: Rouen, Amiens, Lille and Brussels were freed within days.
Lyon was freed; the Germans blew up its bridges as they left.
The armies from Normandy and Provence met in Burgundy; Dijon, Besançon and Nancy were freed.
American troops took Metz; Mulhouse and Belfort fell to the French the same week.
General Leclerc's division entered Strasbourg and raised the French flag on the cathedral.

ending.title: Liberation
ending.epilogue: France is free again, except for a few besieged ports and a corner of Alsace. The prisoners and the deported have not come home yet; many never will.

endings.title: Over the mountains
endings.epilogue: Spain, then Gibraltar or a Spanish camp, then perhaps London. The ones left behind carry on without you.

endings.title: Across the Swiss border
endings.epilogue: Safe, for now, behind the wire of a Swiss camp, with France a few hundred metres away.

endings.title: Taken

when.judged: the player is arrested and taken away by the Gestapo or the French police with no way to escape: in a cell, a car or a train east

endings.epilogue: What happens next is the story of the camps and the prisons. Somewhere, someone else picks up the work.
